title: In crisis-affected communities, prosperity is understood as shared capability, safety, and the ability to plan beyond survival
source_unit: Prosper Global, Voices of Prosperity: What It Means to Prosper, September 2026
geography: 396 individual and group conversations with 1,102 people across Colombia, Democratic Republic of Congo, Indonesia, Kenya, Syria, and Ukraine; local teams conducted conversations in 15 languages

observations.period: 2026 qualitative inquiry; community definitions of prosperity

denominator.unit: people participating in individual and group conversations across six countries

shared_prosperity.value: participants rarely described prosperity as an individual outcome; they connected their wellbeing to family, neighbors, and community progress

relational_condition.value: prosperity is treated as a condition that is weakened when others remain unsafe, excluded, or unable to recover

cultural_consumer_implication.value: a household or individual gain is not experienced as durable prosperity if local social and material systems remain unstable

observations.method: Prosper Global qualitative inquiry using 396 individual and group conversations conducted by local teams in 15 languages across six crisis-affected countries.
observations.uncertainty: The report is purposive qualitative research, not a representative prevalence estimate, standardized cross-country survey, or causal evaluation; translations and local recruitment shape comparability.
observations.subgroup: People living through conflict, climate change, displacement, and economic hardship, with country and community context central to interpretation.
observations.counterinterpretation: Participants’ emphasis on shared prosperity may reflect the crisis settings and the organization’s listening frame rather than a universal rejection of individual advancement.

observations.period: 2026 qualitative inquiry; safety, stability, and future planning

denominator.unit: countries included in the qualitative inquiry

planning_capacity.value: participants described prosperity as the ability to look beyond immediate needs and plan for education, livelihoods, and the future

precondition.value: safety and stability are treated as enabling conditions for future orientation, not merely as outcomes of income growth

time_horizon.value: crisis compresses the time horizon toward survival; prosperity expands practical room to make longer-term choices

observations.method: Cross-site thematic synthesis of participant accounts in the Prosper Global report.
observations.uncertainty: The report does not measure the prevalence or causal effect of planning capacity, nor isolate conflict, climate, displacement, and economic hardship as independent drivers.
observations.subgroup: Displaced people, conflict-affected communities, climate-exposed households, young people facing constrained livelihood opportunities, and families navigating insecurity.
observations.counterinterpretation: Future planning may be a culturally specific expression of aspiration and cannot be assumed to translate into measurable mobility or improved wellbeing without material supports.

observations.period: 2026 qualitative inquiry; local knowledge, mutual support, and self-directed recovery

denominator.unit: individual and group conversations across six countries

community_assets.value: participants emphasized existing knowledge, mutual support, local networks, and shared resources as foundations for prosperity

assistance_boundary.value: outside assistance remains essential in crisis but is not described as sufficient for durable prosperity

agency_route.value: durable recovery depends on locally owned capability and viable livelihoods, not only delivery of relief

observations.method: Local-team qualitative conversations and report synthesis focused on participants’ own definitions of prosperity and support.
observations.uncertainty: The source does not compare assistance models, estimate program effects, or establish that local ownership alone overcomes structural constraints, conflict, or unequal power.
observations.subgroup: Community members, local entrepreneurs, farmers, displaced people, and families relying on local networks amid crisis and economic hardship.
observations.counterinterpretation: Emphasizing community assets can unintentionally shift responsibility from states and international actors onto communities that lack resources or security.

observations.period: 2026 qualitative inquiry; recurring barriers to prosperity

denominator.unit: cross-site barrier families identified by the report

barriers.value: conflict and insecurity, lived climate impacts, and economic hardship recur across the six-country inquiry

youth_opportunity.value: limited opportunities for young people are identified as a particularly persistent economic barrier

compound_exposure.value: security, climate, and livelihood shocks compound by narrowing both present resources and future planning room

observations.method: Thematic synthesis of 396 conversations across Colombia, Democratic Republic of Congo, Indonesia, Kenya, Syria, and Ukraine.
observations.uncertainty: Recurring themes do not show equal intensity across countries or prove that the three barrier families have the same mechanism or policy solution everywhere.
observations.subgroup: Young people, climate-exposed producers, displaced and conflict-affected households, and communities facing constrained access to livelihoods and services.
observations.counterinterpretation: The barrier framework may understate political economy, gender, disability, health, and institutional differences that shape who can convert assistance or local resources into opportunity.

related_sources.claim: Prosper Global initiative page describing the six-country, 15-language listening approach and community-centered definition of prosperity.
Country vignette connecting climate exposure, local livelihood innovation, community support, and shared prosperity in Kenya.

boundary: This record adds a qualitative, community-defined prosperity route linking shared wellbeing, safety, future planning, local knowledge, mutual support, climate exposure, conflict, displacement, and youth opportunity. It is not a representative global survey, respondent-level atlas ingestion, causal evaluation, or proof that community-led approaches substitute for public protection, international assistance, or structural change.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official Prosper Global report page, initiative page, and Kenya country vignette reviewed for sample description, countries, languages, qualitative method, shared-prosperity findings, planning mechanism, local-asset framing, and recurring barriers.
